## Summary

Brazil lived with inflation of several thousand percent a year for a decade. A heavily indexed economy made it bearable, and five price-freeze plans each failed. By the strict 50 %-a-month definition, hyperinflation lasted only from **December 1989 to March 1990**, with a peak of **82.4 % in March 1990, doubling every 35.1 days** (H&K). The Collor plan then froze 80 % of the country's money in bank accounts. The cure that held was the **Plano Real** (1994): a unit of account (the URV) first, the new currency after.

## Causes

- **Indexation everywhere.** Wages, rents, contracts and bonds were adjusted to past inflation, so
  last month's inflation became this month's (inertial inflation).
- **Deficits financed with money**, the external debt crisis of the 1980s, and plans that froze
  prices without fixing the budget.

## Timeline

- **28 Feb 1986** — the Cruzado Plan: a price freeze and the new cruzado.
- **12 Jun 1987** — the Bresser Plan.
- **15 Jan 1989** — the Summer Plan (Plano Verão) and the cruzado novo.
- **Dec 1989** — monthly inflation passes 50 % (H&K start).
- **16 Mar 1990** — the Collor Plan freezes about 80 % of all liquidity in bank accounts; the
  cruzeiro returns. Monthly inflation falls from 81.3 % (March) to 11.3 % (April). It rises again
  after July 1990.
- **1993** — the cruzeiro real.
- **Feb – Jun 1994** — the URV, a virtual unit of account adjusted daily, while prices move to it.
- **1 Jul 1994** — the URV becomes the real.

## The end

The Plano Real fixed what the earlier plans had missed. It did not freeze prices. It first moved every price into a stable unit of account, the URV, and only then turned that unit into money, so indexation unwound on its own.

## Lessons

- Freezing prices or bank deposits treats the symptom; each freeze cost trust for the next plan.
- Stability was rebuilt by changing *expectations* first (the URV), then the money.
